meta.subtitle: Zero to Linux Foundation Certified System Administrator

overview.title: How This Course Works
overview.subtitle: Twelve weeks from first shell prompt to a passing score, on any distro
body: The LFCS is not a multiple-choice exam. You are dropped onto a live Linux system with a list of tasks and a two-hour clock. Nothing is graded on how you did it — only on whether the machine ends up in the required state. That single fact should shape everything about how you study.

So this course is built around doing, not reading. Every week has a focus, a short list of tasks, and a full lab guide with the actual commands, the verification step, and a break/fix drill that forces you to recover from something you broke on purpose. If you finish a week without having typed anything, you haven't finished the week.

The Linux Foundation grades the LFCS independent of distribution — no specific distro is required or assumed. That is the entire reason this course is built the way it is: every lab guide gives you the command for a Debian-family system (Ubuntu) and the command for an RPM-family system (Rocky Linux / RHEL) side by side, so you are never stuck translating mid-task.

rhythm.text: hands-on labs on a machine you can break and rebuild
reading man pages and official docs — the only reference you get in the exam
review — write down every command that didn't work the first time

rows: One week per module. Realistic for a working adult starting near zero.
Two modules per calendar week. Best if you have prior Linux exposure or are job-searching full time.
Stretch each module by half. Better than quitting because the pace was unrealistic.

note.title: Learn the concept, not the distro
note.text: The LFCS will not tell you which distro you're on and won't accept "but that's how Ubuntu does it" as an excuse. Every lab guide in this course drills the same task twice — once with apt/systemd-networkd-style tooling, once with dnf/nmcli-style tooling — until the underlying concept is what you know, not a memorized command line.

exam.title: What the LFCS Actually Is
exam.subtitle: Format, domains, and what the graders care about
body: Knowing the shape of the exam changes how you practise. The LFCS is a performance-based, hands-on exam delivered online and proctored — you solve real command-line tasks on a live system. There are no multiple-choice questions and no partial credit for knowing the theory out loud.

facts.v: Online, proctored, performance-based — command-line tasks on a live system
Independent of distribution — no specific distro required or assumed
man pages and locally installed docs are available; no notes, no books
2 years from the date you pass
Exam purchase includes two exam attempts and two 36-hour simulator sessions, within a 12-month window

domains.title: The five exam domains
rows: Kernel configuration, process management, job scheduling, software maintenance, disaster recovery, virtual machines, containers, SELinux/AppArmor
IPv4/IPv6 addressing, DNS, time synchronization, SSH, packet filtering, routing, bonding, load balancers
LVM, virtual filesystems, filesystem management, remote storage, swap space, storage performance monitoring
Shell fluency, Git, service creation, performance troubleshooting, application resource constraints, SSL certificates
Account management, environment/profile configuration, resource limits, ACLs, LDAP integration

implications.title: What that means for how you study
bullets: Learn the man pages, not one distro's wiki. They're the only reference you get, and they read the same on every distro. Practise man -k and section numbers until they're faster than a search engine would be.
Practise the same task twice, on two families. Once on something Debian-based, once on something RPM-based. If you can only do it one way, you don't know it yet — you've memorized it.
Speed matters, but correctness matters more. A half-finished task scores nothing. Finish and verify each task before moving to the next.
Never memorise a GUI path. Everything in this course runs at the command line, because that's what's reliably available under exam conditions.
There is no partial credit for approach. If ip and nmcli both get the network config right, both are correct. Use whichever you're fastest with.

note.title: Read the objectives yourself — from the source
note.text: The Linux Foundation publishes the full LFCS domain list, and it is the only authoritative statement of what is testable. Everything in this course maps to it. Bookmark it and re-read it in Week 11: training.linuxfoundation.org — LFCS certification details.

homelab.title: Build Your Home Lab
homelab.subtitle: Two virtual machines, a free hypervisor, and two different Linux families — that's the whole setup
body: You need at least two Linux systems you're willing to destroy, and — because this exam is distro-neutral — you get the most out of this course if those two systems come from different families: one Debian-based, one RPM-based. Virtual machines are ideal. They snapshot, they roll back, and breaking one costs you nothing.
A laptop you already own plus a free hypervisor and two free operating system downloads is the entire minimum investment. Everything below assumes that setup.

startHere.title: Start here — the three-step path
steps: Install Ubuntu Server (free, no account) on one VM and Rocky Linux (free, no account) on a second. That single pairing covers both families the exam is built around.
Pick a free hypervisor — Oracle VirtualBox is the default recommendation below — and give each VM 2 vCPU, 2–4 GB RAM, and a 20 GB disk, plus a second empty 10 GB disk for the storage weeks.
Snapshot both machines the moment install finishes. Then break them on purpose, every single week, and put them back.

budgetNote.title: Don't overbuy
budgetNote.text: Two virtual machines on a laptop you already own costs nothing and is enough for the entire exam. Buy hardware only if your current machine can't spare 8 GB of RAM. There is no lab in this course that needs a server, a rack, or a homelab shopping list.

groups.title: Pick a hypervisor and size the VMs
groups.intro: Everything in this course runs on two virtual machines. Any of these will do it — pick the one that matches your hardware and stop researching.

items.name: Oracle VirtualBox
items.desc: The default choice for this course. Free, open source, and runs on Linux, macOS (Intel), and Windows hosts. Snapshots are one click and easy to roll back, which matters — you will break these machines every week. Use the built-in Host-only Adapter for the private lab network.

items.name: VMware Workstation Pro
items.desc: Free for personal use under Broadcom. Noticeably faster disk and network performance than VirtualBox on most hardware. Fusion is the equivalent on Mac.

items.name: KVM / virt-manager
items.desc: If your daily driver is already Linux, this is the fastest, lightest option — and it's the same virtualization stack the exam's own "virtual machines" objective expects you to understand.

items.name: UTM
items.desc: The practical option on Apple Silicon, where VirtualBox doesn't run. Emulates or virtualises aarch64 guests — both Ubuntu and Rocky ship aarch64 images.

groups.title: Get both operating systems
groups.intro: You want one guest from each family. These two, specifically, are what the lab guides in this course are written against.

items.name: Ubuntu Server
items.desc: The Debian family. No account required. Ships apt, netplan/systemd-networkd, and AppArmor — the tooling roughly half of this exam's tasks expect.

items.name: Rocky Linux
items.desc: The RPM family, a free RHEL rebuild. No account required. Ships dnf, NetworkManager/nmcli, and SELinux — the other half of the exam's tooling.

cloud.title: Self-Managed Cloud Hosted Labs
cloud.subtitle: The same two machines on a provider you rent by the hour — for when the laptop can't spare the RAM
body: If your machine can't host two virtual machines, rent them instead. A small instance pair costs roughly $10–20 per month if you leave it running, and far less if you destroy it between study sessions — which you should.

You don't need a custom script for this: create one Ubuntu instance and one Rocky Linux instance from each provider's own console, add a small second data volume to one of them for the storage weeks, and open SSH to your own IP only.

items.name: Google Cloud
items.desc: Both Ubuntu and Rocky Linux images are first-class citizens in the marketplace. New accounts get free trial credit that can cover most of a 12-week run.

items.name: DigitalOcean
items.desc: The simplest pricing of the four, with both distros in the catalogue and block volumes that attach cleanly for the LVM week.

items.name: Amazon Web Services
items.desc: Ubuntu and Rocky AMIs are both available. Free tier covers a small instance pair if you watch the hours.

items.name: Vultr
items.desc: Cheap hourly instances and inexpensive block storage. Often the lowest total cost if you're disciplined about destroying the lab.

after.title: Before you spend anything
bullets: Set a billing alert on day one. Every provider offers one free, and every provider will happily bill you for an instance you forgot about.
Generate an SSH key first: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C 'lfcs-lab'
Destroy the lab when you finish for the week. Stopping an instance still bills you for its disk.

A cloud lab can't practise everything. Console-level work — interrupting the boot process, resetting a lost root password, editing the bootloader — needs a hypervisor where you control the virtual console. Do Week 6 locally even if everything else is hosted.

certs.title: The Certification Ladder
certs.subtitle: Where LFCS sits, and what pairs well with it
body: LFCS is a solid mid-tier credential on its own — distro-neutral, performance-based, and respected wherever a job description says "Linux" without naming a vendor. It also slots cleanly next to a vendor-specific credential like RHCSA if your target employer runs Red Hat, or leads straight into LFCE if you want to keep climbing.

items.name: LPI Linux Essentials
items.why: The gentlest on-ramp there is. If you're genuinely new to Linux and want a cheap, low-pressure way to prove to yourself you can do this before spending $445, this is it.

items.name: Linux Foundation Certified System Administrator
items.why: The certification this entire course is built around. Two hours, live command line, no distro favoritism.

items.name: Red Hat Certified System Administrator
items.why: If your target employer runs Red Hat specifically, RHCSA is the name they'll ask for by name. The overlap with what you've just learned is large — this is largely a vendor-specific dialect of the same skills.

items.name: Linux Foundation Certified Engineer
items.why: The advanced counterpart to LFCS, going deeper on the same distro-neutral philosophy. A current LFCS is generally treated as the on-ramp.

note.title: Skip the extras if you're confident and short on money
note.text: Linux Essentials is a confidence builder, not a prerequisite. If you've sat proctored exams before and money is tight, go straight at LFCS and put the savings toward a retake if you need one.

coverage.title: Exam Domain Coverage Map
coverage.subtitle: All five LFCS domains, mapped to the weeks that cover them
coverage.intro: The Linux Foundation groups the LFCS objectives into five domains. Every one is covered, weighted roughly by how much of the exam it's worth.
columns: What you'll actually be able to do
rows: Shell fluency, redirection and pipes, grep and regex, Git branching/merging, creating a systemd service unit, reading performance counters, generating and reading an SSL certificate
Create/modify/delete users and groups, configure sudo, set environment and shell profiles, apply resource limits with ulimit, set ACLs, bind a system to LDAP for authentication
Manage kernel modules and parameters, install/update/remove packages on both families, schedule work with cron/at/systemd timers, take and restore a backup
Build and manage a local VM, run and manage containers, read and fix an SELinux or AppArmor denial
Partition a disk, build and extend an LVM volume, create and mount ext4/XFS filesystems, mount an NFS share, configure swap, read iostat/vmstat output
Configure IPv4/IPv6 addressing on both families, set up DNS resolution, sync time with chrony/NTP, harden SSH, filter packets, configure static routes, bond interfaces, stand up a basic load balancer

weeks.title: The 12-Week Plan
weeks.subtitle: Check tasks off as you go — your progress is saved in this browser

items.title: Shell, Permissions, and Text Processing
items.summary: The commands you'll use in every other week, drilled on both distro families from day one.
tasks: Navigate the filesystem hierarchy and explain what lives in /etc, /var, /usr, and /home on both distros
Use redirection and pipes fluently: >, >>, |, 2>, 2>&1, and tee
Search text with grep and basic regular expressions — anchors, character classes, and quantifiers
Create, copy, move, and delete files and directories, including recursively and safely
Create hard links and symbolic links, and explain when each breaks
Read and set ugo/rwx permissions in both symbolic and octal form, plus a POSIX ACL with setfacl
Archive and compress with tar, gzip, and bzip2, and unpack all three
Connect to your second machine over SSH and switch users with su and sudo
objectives: Access a shell prompt and issue commands with correct syntax
Use input-output redirection
Use grep and regular expressions to analyze text
Create, delete, copy, and move files and directories
Create hard and soft links
Set and modify standard ugo/rwx permissions and POSIX ACLs
Archive, compress, unpack, and uncompress files
Access remote systems using SSH

items.title: Git, Services, and Performance Troubleshooting
items.summary: The less obvious half of Essential Commands: Git, writing your own systemd unit, and finding what's slow.
tasks: Initialize a Git repo, stage and commit changes, and work with branches and merges
Resolve a merge conflict from the command line
Write a custom systemd service unit and enable it to survive reboot
Use top, ps, and free to identify what's consuming CPU, memory, and swap
Generate a self-signed SSL certificate with openssl and explain what a CSR is
Constrain a process or service with basic resource limits (nice/renice, systemd resource controls)
objectives: Operate a Git repository — init, add, commit, branch, merge, resolve conflicts
Create and manage systemd services and units
Identify CPU, memory, and disk performance bottlenecks
Manage application resource constraints
Generate and manage SSL certificates

items.title: Users, Groups, and Access Control
items.summary: The smallest domain by weight, easy marks if you get sudo, ACLs, and limits right.
tasks: Create, modify, and delete local users and groups on both distro families
Configure passwordless and password-required sudo rules in /etc/sudoers.d/
Set and age passwords, and lock/unlock an account
Configure default environment variables and shell profiles in /etc/profile.d/ and per-user dotfiles
Apply per-user resource limits with ulimit and /etc/security/limits.conf
Set default and non-default ACLs on a shared directory with setfacl and getfacl
Bind a client to an LDAP directory for centralized authentication (SSSD)
objectives: Create, delete, and modify local user accounts
Create, delete, and modify local groups and group memberships
Configure superuser access
Configure user resource limits
Manage file access with ACLs
Configure a system to authenticate using LDAP

items.title: Packages, the Kernel, and Backups
items.summary: Install and update software on both families, work with kernel modules, and back up before you break anything.
tasks: Install, update, and remove packages with apt on Ubuntu and dnf on Rocky
Add and manage a third-party repository on both distros
List, load, and unload kernel modules with lsmod, modprobe, and rmmod
Read and set kernel parameters at runtime and persistently with sysctl
Take a filesystem-level backup with tar or rsync and restore from it
Explain the difference between a full, incremental, and differential backup
objectives: Manage software using distribution-specific package management tools
Manage and configure the Linux kernel and kernel modules
Perform basic system administration tasks including software maintenance
Implement disaster recovery — backup and restore data

items.title: Processes and Scheduled Work
items.summary: Manage what's running and when it runs, from a one-off cron job to a recurring systemd timer.
tasks: List, prioritize (nice/renice), and terminate processes safely
Identify a runaway process and stop it cleanly, then forcefully
Schedule a one-time job with at and a recurring job with cron
Write a systemd timer unit as a cron replacement and explain why you might prefer one
Read and interpret systemd unit dependency chains with systemctl list-dependencies
Boot into and change the default systemd target
objectives: Manage starting, stopping, and debugging of processes and services
Schedule tasks using cron and systemd timers
Manage system startup and change the default target
Monitor and manage running system state

items.title: Virtual Machines, Containers, and SELinux/AppArmor
items.summary: The exam's virtualization and security objectives in one week — build a VM, run a container, fix a denial.
tasks: Install libvirt/KVM and create a small VM from the command line with virt-install
Start, stop, and connect to a VM's console with virsh
Install Docker or Podman and run, stop, and inspect a container
Build a minimal container image from a Dockerfile/Containerfile
Read an SELinux AVC denial in the audit log and fix it with restorecon or a boolean (Rocky)
Read an AppArmor denial and put a profile into enforce or complain mode (Ubuntu)
objectives: Deploy, configure, and maintain virtual machines
Deploy, configure, and maintain containers
Manage and configure SELinux or AppArmor
Diagnose and resolve mandatory access control denials

items.title: Partitions, LVM, and Filesystems
items.summary: This is where the second disk you added in the home lab starts earning its keep.
tasks: List, create, and delete GPT partitions with parted or fdisk
Build a physical volume, volume group, and logical volume with LVM
Extend a logical volume and its filesystem without unmounting it
Create ext4 and XFS filesystems and explain when you'd pick each
Mount a filesystem at boot by UUID via /etc/fstab, on both distros
Add and enable swap space, both as a partition and as a swap file
objectives: Create and configure LVM storage
Create, manage, and troubleshoot filesystems
Manage swap space
Configure and mount local filesystems persistently

items.title: Remote Storage and Performance Monitoring
items.summary: Mount someone else's disk over the network, and learn to read the numbers when storage is the bottleneck.
tasks: Export an NFS share from one lab machine and mount it on the other, persistently
Configure autofs to mount an NFS share on demand
Explain what a virtual filesystem is and inspect /proc and /sys
Read iostat, vmstat, and df/du output to diagnose a storage bottleneck
Find and reclaim disk space consumed by open-but-deleted files
objectives: Manage and configure remote (network) filesystems
Understand and manage virtual filesystems
Monitor storage performance
Diagnose and correct storage-related problems

items.title: IP Addressing, DNS, and SSH
items.summary: The first half of the exam's biggest domain: get two machines talking and resolving names correctly.
tasks: Configure a static IPv4 and IPv6 address with nmcli (Rocky) and netplan/systemd-networkd (Ubuntu)
Configure DNS resolution and explain the systemd-resolved / /etc/resolv.conf relationship
Synchronize system time with chrony and verify sync status
Harden SSH: disable root login, enforce key-based auth, change the listening port
Copy a file between the lab machines with scp and rsync over SSH
Use ss and ip to inspect current connections and interface state
objectives: Configure IPv4 and IPv6 networking
Configure and use DNS resolution
Configure network time synchronization
Configure and secure SSH access
Diagnose and correct networking problems

items.title: Firewalls, Routing, Bonding, and Load Balancing
items.summary: The second half of Networking — everything after the packet leaves the box.
tasks: Filter traffic with firewalld (Rocky) and ufw/nftables (Ubuntu), matching the same rule on both
Add a static route and explain the default route / gateway relationship
Bond two network interfaces and verify failover
Stand up a minimal HTTP load balancer with HAProxy or nginx in front of two backend hosts
Capture and read basic traffic with tcpdump to confirm a rule is actually working
objectives: Implement packet filtering
Configure routes and static routing
Configure network interface bonding
Configure a basic load balancer
Troubleshoot network connectivity issues

items.title: Integration and Break/Fix Week
items.summary: No new material. Combine everything into realistic, multi-step problems and time yourself.
tasks: Run three timed 45-minute drills that each cross at least two domains (e.g. LVM + NFS + a firewall rule)
Roll both lab machines back to a clean snapshot and rebuild the full two-machine topology from scratch
Deliberately break five things — one per domain — without writing down what you did, then diagnose and fix each cold
Re-read the official LFCS domain list end to end and flag anything you can't do without looking it up
objectives: Demonstrate essential commands under time pressure
Demonstrate users and groups tasks under time pressure
Demonstrate operations deployment tasks under time pressure
Demonstrate storage tasks under time pressure
Demonstrate networking tasks under time pressure

items.title: Mock Exam, Remediation, and Exam Day
items.summary: A full timed mock exam under real conditions, remediation of everything you missed, and exam-day logistics.
tasks: Roll both lab machines back to a clean snapshot
Sit a full 2-hour timed mock exam — no notes, no internet, man pages only
Score yourself honestly against the five domains and identify your weakest one
Rebuild the labs for every missed objective, from scratch, untimed
Book the exam and complete the proctoring system check the day before
Sit a second mock in the final 48 hours, then rest
objectives: Complete a full performance-based exam simulation within the time limit
Identify and remediate weak domains
Understand the proctoring and exam-day requirements

labs.title: Lab Guides
labs.subtitle: One standalone guide per week — real commands on both distro families, verification steps, and a break/fix drill
labs.intro: Each guide is self-contained and follows the same shape: what you're building, the commands on Ubuntu and the commands on Rocky, how to verify it, a deliberate break to repair, and a final check. They print cleanly if you'd rather work from paper.

note.title: How to use a lab guide
note.text: Read the whole guide first. Then close it and try the tasks from memory — on both distros if you have both VMs up. Open it again only when you're stuck, and write down what you had to look up. That list is your real study guide for Week 11.

verify.title: Employer Verification
verify.subtitle: This course is free. A verifiable certificate of completion, if you want one, runs through a $20/month subscription you can cancel anytime
body: Everything on this page — all 12 weeks, every lab guide — is free and always will be. It has no login and tracks nothing.

Some employers want more than your word that you did the work. Learn Linux For Work's paid course track wraps this same curriculum in a tracked account, so finishing it produces a certificate an employer can actually check — not just a PDF you made yourself. It's a $20/month subscription, not a one-time purchase: stay enrolled while you work through the weeks, then cancel as soon as you've got your certificate. You keep it either way.

startHere.title: How it works
steps: Join Learn Linux For Work and enroll in the LFCS course track — $20/month, cancel anytime.
Work through the same 12 weeks and tasks on this page, tracked to your account instead of just your browser.

Finish the course and request your certificate — a shareable digital credential for LinkedIn, or a copy printed and mailed to your door. Cancel the subscription once you have it; the certificate is yours to keep.

note.title: The cheapest way to fail
note.text: Booking the exam before you can finish a timed mock cleanly. The LFCS is two hours with no partial credit for approach — sitting it unprepared costs you $445 and a month of momentum. Pass a full mock on both distro families first, then book.

examday.title: Exam Day and Staying On Track
examday.subtitle: The habits that get you there, and the checklist for the morning itself

tips.head: Practise on both families, every week.
tips.text: The single biggest cause of a missed task isn't not knowing the concept — it's only knowing one distro's command for it. Never let a week end with only one family drilled.

tips.head: Keep a break/fix log.
tips.text: Every error you hit and how you fixed it, in a text file on the machine. By Week 11 it becomes your personal study guide.

tips.head: Live in the man pages.
tips.text: They're the only documentation you get, and they read the same everywhere. Practise finding things with man -k until it's faster than searching would be.

tips.head: Break things on purpose.
tips.text: Every lab guide ends with a break/fix drill for a reason. Recovering a broken system under time pressure is the actual skill being tested.

tips.head: Verify, then move on.
tips.text: There's no partial credit. Finishing 15 tasks correctly beats starting 22. Check each one before you leave it.

tips.head: Two hours moves fast.
tips.text: Read every task once before you start any of them. Do the ones you know cold first, and don't let one hard task eat the time for three easy ones.

tips.head: Book the exam to create a deadline.
tips.text: Once you can pass a timed mock on both distro families, book it within two weeks. Open-ended study drifts.

checklist.title: The morning of the exam
bullets: Government-issued photo ID ready — check the name matches your Linux Foundation account exactly.
Test your machine, camera, and internet against the proctoring system check the day before, not the morning of.
Clear your desk completely. No notes, no books, no second monitor, no phone.
First ten minutes: read every task before you start any of them.
Last ten minutes: re-verify anything you rushed. There's no reboot check like RHCSA's, but there is no partial credit either — a task half-done scores the same as not attempted.

note.title: If you don't pass the first time
note.text: It's a real exam and plenty of good administrators don't pass on the first attempt. Your purchase includes a second attempt within 12 months. Work your weakest domain for two weeks, sit another killer.sh session, and go again.

story.title: Why I Built This Guide
story.subtitle: A note from Shea Bennett, founder of Shea's Tech
story.photoAlt: Shea Bennett, founder of Shea's Tech
body: Shea Bennett started his career in Information Technology as a Helpdesk Analyst with no formal training or background in IT. He had no experience when he left the U.S. Navy, where he served as a Hospital Corpsman assigned to a Marine Corps battalion as a Fleet Marine Force (FMF) combat medic. His dream was to become a medical doctor, but the cost of medical education was simply too high — not something the Montgomery GI Bill alone could cover.

While working as a surgical technologist passing instruments at Naval Medical Center San Diego, he met engineers from a healthcare imaging company and asked one of them for help getting into IT. To his surprise, the man helped him land his first real IT job. Shea then spent the next few years training onsite at that company's headquarters in northern New Jersey, flying back and forth from San Diego. He struggled at first — he's a visual learner, and in 2007 the most common way to learn IT was in-person bootcamps or classroom training, neither of which he could afford.

Then he found video-based IT training, and never looked back. Shea is 100% self-taught. He went on to earn a Bachelor's and a Master's degree from National University in San Diego, and trained extensively alongside various government agencies and U.S. government IT contractors. He believes anyone can learn IT on their own without paying for a bootcamp — but that mentorship and networking, in person or on live video, are critical, because IT is a team sport.

This course exists for the same reason the RHCSA and AWS DevOps courses do: the LFCS is the certification employers ask for when they need a Linux administrator but don't want to commit to one vendor's ecosystem. It deserved a free, distro-neutral course to match — one that actually respects the "independent of distribution" promise instead of quietly teaching one distro and hoping it's close enough.
quote: This was built for that fundi in Kenya, that hustler in Nigeria, the determined in Rwanda or Ethiopia. The hungry surviving in the UAE. The Indonesian or Filipino brother or sister — determined, but never given a chance or guidance.
